inserts.title: Tethered headings reveal sustained orientation
paragraphs: A fine wire attached to the dorsal thorax held each monarch in place while it rotated freely. A cylinder roughly 59 cm wide and 64 cm high limited its view to the sky overhead, so the sky was the visual reference available to the insect. Vertical airflow lifted the butterfly without supplying a horizontal wind direction.

The system sampled heading every 200 ms, which recorded both sustained orientation and course changes within a single trial. Virtual trajectories were built from those headings by assuming a flight speed, so the distances shown are calculated rather than measured. Each trial therefore gives a continuous record of the butterfly's chosen direction.

Excluding landscape landmarks allowed solar orientation to be tested under controlled visual access, which isolates the sky as the reference. Because the record is continuous, each trial keeps changes in course as they occur. The sky served as the sole visual reference in each trial. The experiment therefore isolates direction-holding from travel.
notes: Tethered headings reveal sustained orientation.

inserts.title: Opposite clock shifts rotate headings oppositely
paragraphs: Mouritsen and Frost delayed the entraining 12-h light:12-h dark cycle by 6 h, creating the reverse of the advance tested earlier. The delayed group was tested in the same simulator as the autumn migrants, so the apparatus stayed constant while the light schedule changed. The advance and delay therefore differ in their clock phase.

Delayed butterflies oriented near 335°, toward the northwest, a change of about 110° clockwise from the local-time mean of 225°. The advance had produced a counterclockwise change, so the two manipulations moved the heading in opposite directions. Both results come from the same simulator and season. The heading shifts were measured relative to the local-time mean.

Unequal magnitudes between the two shifts reflect the observed solar geometry and the experimental conditions. Opposite shifts from opposite clock manipulations indicate a signed link between clock phase and compass direction. Each manipulation therefore produces a predictable heading change. The sign of the change follows the sign of the clock shift.
notes: Opposite clock shifts rotate headings oppositely.

inserts.title: UV-blocked light still sets emergence timing
paragraphs: Froy and colleagues reared monarch pupae under light–dark cycles with a filter that blocked UV, then recorded eclosion, the emergence of adults from the pupal case. Advancing the filtered schedule by 6 h moved the emergence peaks approximately 5.5 h, which shows that the schedule carried the timing signal. The filter kept UV light out of the rearing chamber.

Emergence remained concentrated at one phase of the daily cycle in these pupae. The timing response occurred without ultraviolet illumination, so visible wavelengths were sufficient to set the daily emergence phase. The emergence peaks moved in step with the filtered schedule. Adults were scored for their emergence phase, so the timing measurement was direct.

The flight disruption caused by the UV filter in adults is a separate observation from the emergence result. Visible wavelengths can carry daily timing information in this preparation, so the wavelength that disrupts flight and the wavelength that sets the clock can differ. Those pupal rhythms are a separate output of circadian timing.
notes: UV-blocked light still sets emergence timing.

inserts.title: Polarizer rotation tested under restricted skylight
paragraphs: Sauman and colleagues fixed monarchs to a tether beneath a linear polarizing filter, which limited the skylight to an 80° field and excluded sight of the sun. Rotating the filter by 90° changed the electric-field orientation of the light available to the animal. The sun itself was kept out of direct view throughout.

Each trial used sequential 5-min records taken before rotation, after rotation, during UV interference below 397 nm, and after the UV filter was removed. Interference frequently produced circling and cut virtual progress by at least 70%. Circling was a common response to UV interference. Virtual progress was the measure of each record.

Removing the UV filter restored sustained directional flight, so the effect reversed with the treatment. Spectral interference also altered flight continuity, which mixes the loss of direction with changes in flight behavior. The restricted arrangement limited what the animal could see. Its heading record reflects the skylight that remained visible.
notes: Polarizer rotation tested under restricted skylight.
Explanation 1.

Rotating the filter by 90° changed the electric-field orientation of the light available to the animal. The sun itself was kept out of direct view throughout.

inserts.title: Emergence rhythm free-runs in constant darkness
paragraphs: Froy and colleagues entrained monarch pupae to a light–dark schedule and then exposed them to three conditions: continued cycling light, constant darkness and constant light. Adult emergence time was recorded in each condition. The three conditions tested whether the rhythm needed daily light cues. Emergence timing was the readout across all three conditions.

Eclosion clustered early in the light phase and remained rhythmic in constant darkness, which shows that the rhythm persisted once daily lights were removed. A 6-h shift in the prior light schedule altered the emergence phase. Constant light disrupted the normal temporal concentration of emergence. Emergence timing reflected the light schedule each pupa experienced.

Continuous light disrupted the timing that darkness preserved, so light exposure changes the emergence pattern. Free-running rhythms proceed without daily entrainment, and emergence therefore measures an endogenous timing output. Light exposure therefore changes the emergence timing that darkness keeps. Persistent timing in the dark is evidence of an internal oscillator.
notes: Emergence rhythm free-runs in constant darkness.

Adult emergence time was recorded in each condition. The three conditions tested whether the rhythm needed daily light cues. Emergence timing was the readout across all three conditions.

inserts.title: CRY1 knockdown blocks light-driven TIM decline
paragraphs: Zhu and colleagues used cultured monarch DpN1 cells and RNA interference to lower CRY1 expression. Control cells received interference directed against green fluorescent protein, which served as the reference treatment. Protein levels were measured after the light exposure time course. Cultured cells allow the light response to be examined in isolation.

Under the control treatment, TIM decreased during the light-exposure time course before PER and CRY2 decreased. The cry1 interference prevented this normal light-dependent decline of TIM, the TIMELESS clock protein. CRY1 knockdown therefore changes the light response of TIM. The TIM result is a protein measurement rather than an RNA one.

These protein measurements support CRY1-dependent light input to clock regulation. Brain labeling places CRY1 alongside PER in candidate clock cells, which connects the cell-culture result to the brain. CRY1 is thus a light-responsive input to the clock. The cell-culture result has a brain counterpart in the same cell group.
notes: CRY1 knockdown blocks light-driven TIM decline.

inserts.title: CRY2 knockdown raises reporter activity
paragraphs: Zhu and colleagues reduced endogenous CRY2 in DpN1 cells with RNA interference and set the results against a control sequence. Protein measurements confirmed that the targeted regulator was depleted. Each treatment used the same culture system and reporter readout. Knockdown acted on endogenous CRY2 in these cells. Knockdown was measured at the protein and RNA levels.

CRY2 reduction increased reporter activity about threefold. Across a 24-h light–dark cycle, per RNA remained near its peak values after cry2 interference, instead of following the rise and fall seen in controls. The control cells showed the normal daily rise and fall. The knockdown therefore changed both reporter and RNA rhythms.

The loss-of-function result matches the gain-of-function assay, in which added CRY2 reduced transcription. Together, the two tests show negative feedback, with clock-associated proteins restraining the transcription that produces them. Adding CRY2 suppressed transcription in one test, and removing it raised transcription in the other. The two experiments point the same way.
notes: CRY2 knockdown raises reporter activity.

inserts.title: CRY2 fibers in the central body vary daily
paragraphs: The central body is part of the insect central complex, a set of brain neuropils linked to orientation. Neuropils are regions dense with neuronal processes and synaptic connections, so they can carry signals between cell groups. Zhu and colleagues found CRY2-containing fibers in this region.

The maximum CRY2 staining occurred near CT15, and the minimum occurred near CT9, both measured in constant darkness. Heinze and Reppert's synapsin labeling identifies the central-complex anatomy in which these fibers sit. Staining varied with clock phase in constant darkness. The fiber signal was measured across circadian time. The timing of the maximum and minimum differs by six circadian hours.

A rhythmic protein signal in an orientation-associated region suggests a possible route from clock state to compass processing. Establishing that route depends on identifying the connected cells and manipulating their signal during compass recording. Recording compass output during manipulation tests that connection directly. The link would be tested by manipulating those cells during recording.
notes: CRY2 fibers in the central body vary daily.

inserts.title: Antennal clock RNA rhythms persist in darkness
paragraphs: Merlin and colleagues measured clock-associated RNA in isolated monarch antennae across a light–dark cycle. The transcripts were per, tim and cry2, and cry1 was assessed alongside them. Quantitative PCR converts RNA to DNA so that abundance can be estimated for each sequence. The quantitative assay therefore reports transcript abundance across the cycle.

Antennal per, tim and cry2 RNA varied across the cycle and continued to vary after transfer to constant darkness. Levels were lower near ZT6 than near ZT18, while cry1 RNA showed no such phase difference. Their rhythms persisted without the light cycle present. Levels changed across the day in the cycling condition.

A molecular clock program is present in the appendages needed for normal orientation. Rhythms that continue in darkness point to endogenous timing rather than a direct response to light onset, and they come from the antenna itself. Quantitative PCR measured these transcripts in the same isolated samples. Tissue-level measurements therefore underlie this rhythm claim.
notes: Antennal clock RNA rhythms persist in darkness.

inserts.title: Black antennal paint shifts the selected heading
paragraphs: Merlin and colleagues coated the antennae with black or clear enamel. Black paint blocked transmission across the tested 300–800 nm range, while clear paint kept transmission high and served as the control for the painting procedure. Both coatings left the appendage physically present. Both groups were tested at the same later-autumn season.

Black-painted butterflies chose an abnormal northward bearing near 344° on the normal schedule. Delayed black-painted animals lost group organization, with directions disorganized across the group rather than sharing one heading. The 344° bearing sits well north of the clear-painted mean. Delayed black-painted groups showed no coherent direction. Their abnormal heading shows the effect of blocked antennal light.

Clear-painted animals kept a consistent heading and moved it after a 6-h delay, shifting from about 162° to 269°. The paint result connects antennal light access to time-compensated orientation. The clear-painted shift is the reference against which black-painted animals were judged. Its magnitude was about 107°. Antennal light access is therefore a determinant of the selected heading.
notes: Black antennal paint shifts the selected heading.

Merlin and colleagues coated the antennae with black or clear enamel

inserts.title: Removing a conflicting antenna restores bearing
paragraphs: Guerra and colleagues first flew migrants with one black-painted and one clear-painted antenna, which produced disorganized group headings. The black-painted appendage was then removed, and flight was tested again in the same animals. The same animal therefore carried both conditions in turn. That sequence keeps the individual constant across conditions.

The previously disorganized animals regained a southwest group heading near 214°. Combining repeated-flight controls with first-flight removal controls gave a mean near 216°, which reduces the chance that simulator experience explains the recovery. Removing the black-painted antenna restored a common bearing. The group mean moved to a value close to the earlier southwest headings.

Removing a conflicting timing source restored a consistent bearing, which supports coordinated input from both antennae. The effect depends on which source is removed, and the clear antenna stayed available throughout the intervention. The clear antenna carried the timing signal through both phases. Coordinated input supports the recovery.
notes: Removing a conflicting antenna restores bearing.

inserts.title: Compass neurons prefer specific E-vector angles
paragraphs: Heinze and Reppert recorded identified compass neurons while presenting polarized 365-nm UV light from above. The E-vector rotated through 360° at 30° or 60° per second, so every polarization angle was presented during the recording. Each sweep covered the full polarization axis during the recording.

Action potentials, brief electrical spikes, occurred at different rates for different E-vector angles. The preferred and suppressed axes sat about 90° apart, and the response repeated after 180°, matching the axial symmetry of linear polarization. Intracellular traces kept voltage and time calibration. Responses to each angle were measured in the same cell.

Neurons in this circuit are sensitive to the polarization axis under controlled stimulation. Behavioral masking addresses a different question, because it tests whether the input drives orientation during flight. Lab tuning curves give the expected response to each E-vector angle.
notes: Compass neurons prefer specific E-vector angles.

inserts.title: Migrants show narrower green-light tuning
paragraphs: Nguyen and colleagues recorded tangential neurons from autumn migrants and from non-migratory monarchs. A green 530-nm light spot rotated around the animal at 30° elevation, and the angular range producing elevated spike rates was measured. The angular range is a direct measure of tuning width.

Full width at half maximum gives the width of a tuning curve at half its peak response. Migrants averaged about 83°, and non-migrants averaged about 118°. Peak firing rates were broadly similar, so migrants differed mainly in how narrowly they selected direction. Full width at half maximum is a standard width measure for tuning curves.

The narrower tuning is associated with migratory condition in these recordings. Wild migrants and commercially sourced non-migrants differed in origin and rearing, so the link between tuning and migration is an association between two groups. Narrower tuning therefore characterizes the migrants in this data set. Peak rates contributed less to the difference than width did.
notes: Migrants show narrower green-light tuning.

inserts.title: Cold exposure produces northward headings
paragraphs: Guerra and Reppert exposed fall migrants to 24 days of conditions resembling the overwintering environment, at 11°C during the light phase and 4°C during darkness. Both treatments included cold, but one gradually increased day length while the other kept a constant 12-h light:12-h dark cycle. Those conditions simulate the overwintering thermal regime.

Both cold-treated groups oriented near 358° after warming enough to fly. Warm-housed animals retained a southwest direction near 227°. The northward orientation appeared with or without the changing photoperiod. Northward headings were measured after the animals warmed enough to fly. The warm group's southwest heading was the reference for that response.

The 24-day treatment provides an effective exposure for inducing the reversal in these experiments. Cold therefore acts as an environmental trigger, while time-compensated sun orientation remains available after the switch. The duration of exposure was 24 days, which set the exposure used here. Cold exposure tested here was a sufficient trigger in these conditions.
notes: Cold exposure produces northward headings.

2: Eastern North American monarch butterflies migrate toward overwintering sites in central Mexico, and some journeys exceed 3,500 km. Each migrant's **bearing** is a direction measured around the horizon relative to geographic north. Autumn migrants in this population hold a southwest bearing for the length of the journey. The heading is held across the whole autumn flight.

Mouritsen and Frost recorded autumn migrants in an outdoor flight simulator that allowed turning around a vertical tether. Under a visible sky, the butterflies held southwest headings, with a group mean of 225° when their light schedule matched local time. That mean gives one shared direction for the autumn flight. The local-time schedule produced this southwest group mean.

A **sun compass** uses the position of the sun as a reference for direction. Sustained tethered headings show that this orientation operates even though the butterfly never travels. A southwest bearing describes the chosen direction, which is one component of a full migration. Solar direction serves as the reference, so the chosen bearing is set relative to the sun.
3: A fine wire attached to the dorsal thorax allowed each butterfly to rotate freely. A cylinder about 59 cm wide and 64 cm high restricted its view to the sky above, so the insect turned in place while seeing the sky alone. Vertical airflow supported flight without supplying a horizontal wind direction. The sky above served as the visual reference.

The apparatus sampled heading every 200 ms, which preserved sustained orientation and changes in course during each trial. Each trial therefore captured the course changes made by one individual. Heading records of this kind separate heading control from forward travel in the simulator. Every heading was logged in one continuous record, so each course can be read as a trace.

Virtual trajectories were reconstructed from the recorded headings by assuming a flight speed. Their distances are calculated paths rather than measured displacement. Landscape landmarks were excluded, so solar orientation could be tested under controlled visual access. Heading records alone give direction, and the distance is derived from an assumed speed.
4: A steady tethered heading could arise from a hidden mark on the simulator rather than from a geographic cue. Mouritsen and Frost therefore rotated the whole apparatus, and rotated its components separately, during directional flight. The test asked whether the heading followed the apparatus or the sky. Each rotation tested one possible source of the heading.

Butterflies kept their heading toward the geographic direction rather than following the new apparatus orientation. When an individual was turned manually away from its established heading, it returned toward the previous geographic direction. Sustained orientation appeared despite the absence of forward movement. The heading trace recorded that return in full.

These controls rule out explanations based on a fixed mark, mechanical asymmetry or the tether's angular position. A manipulation that changes internal time while the same external sky stays in view can distinguish time-compensated solar orientation from a response driven by the current sun position alone. The control results therefore constrain the cue to the sky.
5: **Time compensation** adjusts compass output as the sun changes position during the day. A **circadian clock** is an internal timing system with a rhythm close to 24 h, and entrainment aligns its phase with a recurring environmental cycle. The compass corrects its solar reading using that internal schedule. The compass must correct for that shift.

Migrants experienced a 12-h light:12-h dark cycle advanced by 6 h for at least five days. Tested outdoors under the same actual sky as local-time controls, the advanced group oriented near 136°, toward the southeast, instead of the controls' 225° southwest heading. The advanced group therefore faced a different time of day than the controls did.

The counterclockwise change of roughly 89° links orientation to internal time. An insect that treats the afternoon sun as a later time must select a different bearing to keep its programmed compass relationship. The manipulation supports a time-compensated sun compass in which clock output corrects the solar angle. Its direction matches the clock shift.
6: A reciprocal manipulation tests whether the heading change matches the direction predicted by solar time compensation. Mouritsen and Frost delayed the entraining 12-h light:12-h dark cycle by 6 h before testing autumn migrants in the same simulator. The delay produced the opposite clock phase from the advance. Its delay runs opposite to the advance.
